Narrowing appears to originate from the success only reward through the group-relative training advantage to the attacker update, with a persistent success edge setting the direction.
items.title: Tracing Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming

items.summary: Primal-Shortened Information-Set Decoding (ISD) with quadratic polar lifting recently pushed TII McEliece Track-2 key recovery to $mt=126$ (TII-228, $2{,}463$ CPU core-hours), with over $99\%$ of runtime spent harvesting weight-$(2t+1)$ codewords. Porting MiniMax's Mode-6 Stern sampler directly to one block per SM leaves $1.0\text{-}1.5\text{ GB}$ of hash tables active and stalls on global memory. We pack $128$ syndrome bits into one $16$-byte ulonglong2 without left-triple indices (lossless for $mt \le 145$, and extended to $mt \le 192$ via truncated range pre-filtering), share $G \in \{4, 8\}$ cooperative tables inside GPU L2 cache, batch $64G$ random systematic reductions per launch, and widen the shortening prefix $n'$ to cut modeled GPU-hours by $34\%\text{-}47\%$. Across five Track-2 challenges ($mt = 108 \to 153$), every recovered private key passes both the official SageMath checker and a standalone pure-Python verifier. Eight Modal L40S GPUs solve TII-228 ($mt=126$) in $18.9\text{ min}$ ($2.15$ GPU-hours, $3.0\times$ faster in wall-clock than MiniMax's EPYC cluster). We further recover keys for the previously undocumented challenges TII-237 ($mt=135$, $22.1$ L4 GPU-hours), TII-235 ($mt=144$, $39.62$ L40S GPU-hours, $17.97\text{ s}$ lift), and TII-185 ($mt=153$, $140.4$ L40S + $\approx 60$ L4 GPU-hours, $39.01\text{ s}$ lift). These results do not demonstrate practical recovery against Classic McEliece parameters ($mt \ge 768$).
items.title: Packing Stern into L2: GPU-Accelerated Primal-Shortened ISD for High-Codimension Binary Goppa Key Recovery

items.summary: System provenance graphs help reconstruct attacks through causal dependencies, but these connections alone do not explain how events accomplish an adversary's goal. Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) provides the necessary security knowledge, yet linking it to execution evidence requires bridging differences in meaning and granularity between events and attack relations amid scarce labels and sparse relevant evidence. We present LODESTONE, a cross-graph alignment system that links observed system events to CTI attack relations to support evidence-grounded attack reports. LODESTONE uses a novel CTI-driven training-data engine and an expert-verified benchmark of edge-level correspondences and reference attack reports. The engine pairs real CTI knowledge graphs with provenance graphs from isolated executions. A large language model (LLM) agent recursively improves correspondences by checking execution evidence and repairing retrieval, parsing, and reproduction failures; experts independently verify benchmark correspondences. LODESTONE combines text cross-encoder and directed-graph relevance scores to extract compact alert-centered subgraphs, retrieves article-level knowledge graphs through node- and edge-level dual-softmax assignment, and uses a fine-tuned 4B-parameter LLM to align event combinations with CTI attack steps. We evaluate LODESTONE on 27 expert-verified attack cases amid continuous benign activity from real applications, using 713 CTI articles. LLM judgments aligned with multiple human experts yield an attack-step description score of 82%, and attack identification reaches 91%, versus 73% and 32% using the same generator with provenance alone. Baseline pipelines and coding agents achieve description scores of at most 57%. Human-verified correspondences further demonstrate advantages in balancing attack-edge coverage with subgraph size, CTI retrieval, and cross-graph alignment.
items.title: LODESTONE: Linking System Events to Threat Intelligence for Evidence-Grounded Cyber Attack Investigation

items.summary: We propose a new coding-theoretic problem motivated by censorship resistance. Is it possible to intertwine many pieces of data by encoding them jointly in a way that makes it impossible to remove any single piece without destroying many others as well? In particular, we want to encode $k$ data components $(m_1,\ldots, m_k)$ into a codeword $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ with the following properties: 1. Local recovery: every data component can be recovered (in the absence of erasures or errors) by reading at most $\ell$ correct codeword symbols. 2. Unshardability: if an adversary erases some arbitrary subset of the codeword symbols, the remaining codeword symbols either uniquely determine all $k$ data components, or there are at least $s$ data components that cannot be determined. We call such codes $(\ell, s)$-unshardable. Intuitively, such codes prevent an adversary from selectively censoring individual pieces of data by erasing codeword symbols, without destroying large amounts of other data as collateral damage. We show that codes whose generator matrix has certain superregularity properties are unshardable. Using this connection, we construct linear codes that are $(\ell, s)$-unshardable with $s = (1-\varepsilon)k$ and locality $\ell = O_\varepsilon(1)$. We also show that linear unshardable codes are subject to the lower bound $s \leq k - k/\ell + 1$. Finally, we consider a strengthening of local recovery to also require local decodability from some constant fraction of erasures or even errors. With the help of AI tools, we achieve the above notion by showing that any Locally Decodable Code (LDC) can be converted into one that is unshardable while preserving locality via a certain careful change of basis over an appropriate extension field.
items.title: Unshardable Codes
